content:
Apple must respond by Monday to a complaint filed by Epic Games with Brazil's antitrust regulator. Epic accuses Apple of adopting a restrictive interpretation of its obligations under a recent App Store antitrust settlement in Brazil. Details below.

Background

Two months ago, Apple announced that developers can now distribute apps in Brazil through alternative app marketplaces.

This change was part of a settlement that ended a years-long antitrust investigation. The investigation stemmed from a complaint filed by Latin American e-commerce giant MercadoLibre over Apple's App Store rules.

Under the new rules, developers in Brazil can distribute iOS apps through alternative app marketplaces and offer payment methods that bypass Apple's IAP system.

Apple also introduced a new commission structure, including a 5% "Core Technology Fee" on digital goods and services sold through apps distributed outside the App Store. You can read more about the structure here.

Epic challenges Apple's implementation

According to Brazil's O Globo (via MacMagazine) today, Epic recently filed a petition with Brazilian antitrust regulator CADE, accusing Apple of setting up "structural, technical, and entry barriers" that undermine the practical viability of alternative app distribution.

Epic pointed out that while Brazil's new terms only apply to iOS apps, Apple's agreement with CADE "expressly covers iPadOS."

The company is also reportedly objecting to so-called "scare screens" designed to discourage users from installing apps from outside the App Store. Meanwhile, Epic is also opposing the current installation flow, claiming it requires nine steps, compared with six steps in Apple's current implementation in Europe.

O Globo reported that Epic added that Apple's initial installation flow in Europe required 15 steps, but after being forced to reduce it to six steps, the "download abandonment rate dropped from 65% to 25%."

Finally, Epic told CADE that Apple's reporting requirements "far exceed what is needed to calculate fees," arguing that this allows Apple to "monitor competitors' business models."

O Globo said CADE has given Apple until Monday to submit a response. Apple has not publicly commented on the matter.
